# Nasdaq-100 Growth & Momentum Screen — Executive Research Report

**Cohort:** 11 names that passed a 7-factor growth-momentum screen (revenue growth >10% YoY, earnings growth >10% YoY, positive FCF, price > MA50 > MA200, positive 6m return, RSI >40).
**Scope note:** This is commentary on growth durability and price momentum only. No valuation judgment is made; that is left to a separate reverse-DCF stage. Nothing below is a recommendation.

---

## 1. Company-by-company assessment

### MU — Micron Technology
**Growth driver / durability:** Revenue +345.7% and earnings +1,368.5% YoY are extreme outliers even within this cohort. Recent coverage confirms memory (DRAM/NAND, and specifically HBM for AI) prices have stabilized and Micron is adding HBM capacity to meet AI demand — a genuine tailwind. But growth of this magnitude is arithmetic against a cyclical trough in memory pricing from the prior downturn, not evidence of a new steady-state growth rate. This is the textbook base-effect case the screen brief warns about.
**Momentum:** Price (975.26) sits comfortably above MA50 (928.61), which sits far above MA200 (621.93) — a strong, confirmed uptrend. RSI 51.32 is neutral. The 12-month return of +548.75% reflects a full re-rating from trough conditions; price has already moved a long way, and further gains now depend on HBM demand and pricing discipline holding, not on repeating last year's base-effect arithmetic.
**Risks:** Memory is the most historically cyclical semiconductor sub-sector (boom/bust pricing); a new Intel-backed competitor was flagged in coverage; capacity additions across the industry could pressure future pricing; customer base is concentrated among large cloud/AI buyers.

### TER — Teradyne
**Growth driver / durability:** Revenue +103.9%, earnings +385.8%. News points to AI data-center test demand and UltraFLEXplus product growth as drivers, with positive Q3 guidance. As with MU, part of this growth is a recovery from a semiconductor capital-equipment downturn — a partial base effect layered on top of a real AI-testing demand increase.
**Momentum:** Price (379.72) above MA50 (365.69) above MA200 (320.37); RSI 51.49 neutral. But one source notes the stock lost 15.4% in a month — a reminder that the trend, while intact on the moving averages, has seen recent volatility/profit-taking. 12m return of +229.23% again reflects cyclical re-rating rather than steady compounding.
**Risks:** Semiconductor capex is highly cyclical; customer base concentrated among large chipmakers; competitive pressure in automated test equipment.

### AMD — Advanced Micro Devices
**Growth driver / durability:** Revenue +50.1%, earnings +159.5%. Coverage cites new chip architectures aimed at high-performance computing and data centers as the growth engine. The earnings-to-revenue growth gap (roughly 3x) indicates meaningful operating-leverage/margin recovery layered on top of genuine share gains — durable if AI/data-center demand continues, but the magnitude is flattered by a smaller prior profit base.
**Momentum:** RSI 62.56 (firmer than most peers); price (516.13) above MA50 (496.55) above MA200 (346.91) — trend well confirmed. 6m return +166.89%, 12m +231.55%. One source notes the stock pulled back from a ~$584.90 high before forming a bullish continuation pattern, i.e., price has already run hard and is currently consolidating.
**Risks:** Intense competition (Nvidia in AI GPUs, Intel in CPUs); dependence on a concentrated set of hyperscaler customers; a single product-cycle (data-center GPU/CPU refresh) carries much of the growth.

### MRVL — Marvell Technology
**Growth driver / durability:** Revenue +36.5%, earnings +50.0% — the smallest gap between the two in the AI-semi group, suggesting less pure base-effect distortion than MU/TER/AMD. Coverage cites AI-infrastructure partnerships, S&P 500 index inclusion, and a custom-silicon relationship as drivers, alongside a CFO transition and reported insider selling — the latter two flagged in coverage as signs that expectations may be running ahead of the business.
**Momentum:** RSI 49.56, neutral. Price (236.10) above MA50 (216.84) above MA200 (154.76) — trend intact. 6m return +168.92% and 12m +255.31% are large relative to the fundamental growth rates above, indicating the market has re-rated the stock faster than the reported numbers alone would justify.
**Risks:** Customer concentration in a small number of large AI/custom-silicon contracts (explicitly noted in coverage); competition from in-house hyperscaler chip efforts; recent leadership transition (CFO) adds a governance question mark.

### NVDA — NVIDIA
**Growth driver / durability:** Revenue +105.9%, earnings +127.8% — still high, but on a much larger revenue base than MU/TER/AMD, so less likely to be a pure base-effect artifact. Coverage notes continuing AI infrastructure demand as the underlying driver, alongside a cash dividend announcement and flags on competitive dynamics.
**Momentum:** RSI 52.57, neutral. Price (218.29) is only marginally above MA50 (212.36), and MA50 only marginally above MA200 (197.11) — the weakest trend cushion in the cohort. 6m return +21.38% and 12m +23.5% are modest compared with the other AI-semi names, suggesting the market has already priced in much of the growth and the stock is consolidating rather than re-rating further.
**Risks:** Rising competition, including from custom-silicon efforts at hyperscalers and from peers in this same cohort (AMD, Marvell); customer concentration among a handful of large AI infrastructure buyers whose capex plans could shift.

### PLTR — Palantir Technologies
**Growth driver / durability:** Revenue +92.8%, earnings +215.4%. Independent coverage confirms Q2 revenue growth of roughly 93% YoY — a genuine, software-model growth number rather than an obvious hardware-cycle base effect. The earnings growth well above revenue growth suggests the company is still scaling profitability off a comparatively small profit base, which itself is a form of base effect on the bottom line even if top-line growth looks organic.
**Momentum:** RSI 40.78 — the lowest in the cohort, sitting right at the screen's threshold, a sign of fading short-term momentum. Price (167.23) is only slightly above MA50 (153.93), and MA50 only slightly above MA200 (151.52) — a thin trend. 6m return is just +10.79% and 12m return only +1.75%, a marked divergence from the still-strong reported fundamental growth. One source explicitly notes a rating downgrade citing a lack of near-term catalysts.
**Risks:** Customer concentration (government-heavy contracts per coverage); execution risk in commercial expansion; competitive pressure from lower-cost alternatives; and a momentum profile that has stalled even as reported growth remains high.

### AMZN — Amazon.com
**Growth driver / durability:** Revenue +19.6% is the most moderate top-line number in the cohort; earnings +242.3% is disproportionately larger, indicating the growth story here is primarily margin expansion (consistent with a large, diversified retail + cloud business improving profitability) rather than top-line re-acceleration. This combination — modest revenue growth, outsized earnings growth — is arguably the most structurally durable pattern in the group, precisely because it is not dependent on a single cyclical snap-back.
**Momentum:** RSI 48.02, neutral. Price (256.78) is only just above MA50 (255.25), with MA50 comfortably above MA200 (239.8) — a thin, unconfirmed near-term trend sitting on top of an established longer-term one. 6m return +23.65%, but 12m return only +11.67% — momentum is grinding rather than running.
**Risks:** Cloud competition from other large infrastructure providers; regulatory/antitrust scrutiny; consumer-spending cyclicality in the retail segment. Search results returned only generic aggregator pages for AMZN — no specific incremental catalyst could be verified from the tool.

### ADI — Analog Devices
**Growth driver / durability:** Revenue +39.6%, earnings +163.5%. The large gap again points to margin recovery from a cyclical trough in analog/industrial semiconductors, combined with contribution from the Alif acquisition cited in coverage, alongside a broader "AI-growth narrative." Part of this growth is therefore M&A-assisted and cyclical-recovery-assisted rather than purely organic and secular.
**Momentum:** RSI 55.64. Price (378.78) sits only just above MA50 (374.47), with MA50 comfortably above MA200 (349.09) — a modest cushion above trend. 6m return +24.47%, 12m return +54.49% — solid but far more measured than the AI-semi names above.
**Risks:** Analog/industrial end markets (auto, industrial capex) are cyclical; integration risk from the Alif acquisition; competition from other analog semiconductor suppliers.

### FANG — Diamondback Energy
**Growth driver / durability:** Revenue +52.5%, earnings +179.5%. This is the only non-technology name in the cohort. Growth here is best explained as a function of production volumes and/or realized commodity prices rather than any secular demand story — the earnings-over-revenue growth gap again suggests operating leverage from a prior down-period in oil & gas, a classic commodity cycle pattern rather than durable growth in the technology sense.
**Momentum:** RSI 40.71 — tied for the lowest in the cohort, right at the screen threshold. Price (204.97) above MA50 (196.63) above MA200 (180.23) confirms the trend, but 6m return of only +13.63% against a 12m return of +51.65% shows momentum has slowed materially over the most recent half-year. One source explicitly noted the stock "broke out without a clear catalyst."
**Risks:** Full exposure to oil & gas price and volume cyclicality; regulatory/environmental risk; growth here is fundamentally commodity-cycle driven, not comparable in nature to the technology names in this cohort.

### AAPL — Apple
**Growth driver / durability:** Revenue +16.4%, earnings +28.7% — the most modest growth pair in the entire cohort, consistent with a very large, mature revenue base. That this is the lowest growth rate that still clears the screen's 10% thresholds signals deceleration under the weight of scale rather than any re-acceleration. Coverage centers on an upcoming iPhone event, a CEO transition, new device pricing, and rising AI competition — none of these confirm a change in the underlying growth trajectory.
**Momentum:** RSI 70.62 — the highest in the cohort, in overbought territory. Price (332.27) is well above MA50 (317.83), itself well above MA200 (284.54) — a strong trend, but the RSI level suggests the price has moved up quickly in the near term, plausibly on anticipation of the iPhone event and leadership-change speculation rather than in confirmation of a step-change in fundamentals. 6m return +33.08%, 12m return +44.98%.
**Risks:** Leadership transition uncertainty; competitive positioning in AI versus other large-cap peers in this cohort; continued dependence on a single flagship product cycle (iPhone); regulatory pressure in the EU.

### MSFT — Microsoft
**Growth driver / durability:** Revenue +17.7%, earnings +31.7% — similar profile to Apple: modest, mature-base growth rather than reacceleration. Coverage attributes recent share strength to AI demand and plans to expand data-center infrastructure, with the same source flagging spending and execution risk from that build-out.
**Momentum:** RSI 57.49. Price (495.63) above MA50 (453.12) above MA200 (429.65) — a strong, confirmed uptrend. However, 6m return of +25.81% against a 12-month return of essentially flat (-0.26%) shows that the past year has been close to a round trip in price terms, and the recent six-month gain looks more like a bounce than a sustained multi-quarter re-rating — a clear divergence from the other AI-exposed names in the cohort, which show much larger 12-month gains.
**Risks:** Heavy AI infrastructure capex creates execution and margin risk (flagged directly in coverage); competition in cloud/AI; dependence on continued enterprise IT spending.

---

## 2. Cross-cutting risk themes

- **Cyclical base effects (MU, TER, and to a lesser extent AMD/ADI/FANG):** where earnings growth vastly exceeds revenue growth, the arithmetic is often a smaller prior-year profit base (margin recovery from a trough), not a repeatable growth rate. MU is the clearest instance in this cohort.
- **Customer/contract concentration (MRVL, AMD, NVDA, PLTR):** growth in the AI-infrastructure names is tied to a relatively small number of large buyers (hyperscalers, government agencies), making the growth path lumpier and more contract-dependent than the headline percentages suggest.
- **Single product-cycle dependence (AAPL, and to a degree AMD):** growth and near-term momentum are tied to a specific upcoming release or refresh rather than a broad, diversified demand base.
- **Sector-specific cyclicality (FANG):** growth here follows a commodity price/volume cycle, structurally different in kind from the technology names in this screen.
- **Momentum/fundamentals divergence:** PLTR and FANG both show RSI at or near the 40 threshold with 6-month returns well below their 12-month pace — a sign that price momentum has cooled even where reported growth remains elevated. MSFT shows the opposite kind of divergence: a strong recent 6-month bounce sitting on top of a flat 12-month return.

---

## 3. Closing ranking — conviction in the durability of growth

This ranking orders the cohort from highest to lowest conviction that the *reported growth rate* reflects a repeatable business dynamic rather than a cyclical snap-back, M&A effect, or narrow contract dependency. It is **not** a ranking of stock attractiveness, momentum, or score.

| Rank | Ticker | Screen score | Durability reasoning |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | MSFT | 30.3 | Lowest growth rate in the cohort, but from the most diversified, largest base; growth is broad-based rather than tied to one product or cycle. |
| 2 | AMZN | 48.5 | Moderate top-line growth with earnings growth driven by margin expansion across a diversified retail/cloud base — a durable pattern precisely because it is not a snap-back. |
| 3 | NVDA | 51.5 | Growth remains high on a large base and is tied to broad AI infrastructure demand, though price/return momentum already shows signs of deceleration. |
| 4 | ADI | 48.5 | Growth is real but partly M&A-assisted (Alif) and partly a cyclical recovery in analog/industrial end markets. |
| 5 | AAPL | 30.3 | Very stable but low growth, dependent on a single upcoming product cycle and a leadership transition; momentum (RSI 70.6) currently running ahead of the modest fundamental growth. |
| 6 | AMD | 63.6 | Genuine share gains in data-center/HPC chips, but a large earnings-over-revenue growth gap signals meaningful margin-recovery/base-effect contribution; competitive intensity is high. |
| 7 | PLTR | 51.5 | Independently confirmed organic revenue growth, but concentrated customer base and a recent stall in price momentum despite continued fundamental growth. |
| 8 | MRVL | 54.5 | Fast growth but reliant on a small number of large AI/custom-silicon contracts, explicitly flagged as a concentration risk in coverage, with insider-selling noted as a caution. |
| 9 | TER | 78.8 | Growth substantially reflects a recovery in the semiconductor capital-equipment cycle; AI-linked test demand is real but layered on a cyclical rebound. |
| 10 | FANG | 48.5 | Growth is commodity price/volume driven, a fundamentally different (and more cyclical) kind of "growth" than the technology names in this cohort. |
| 11 | MU | 93.9 | The starkest base-effect case in the cohort: triple-digit growth is arithmetic against a cyclical trough in memory pricing, even though a genuine AI/HBM demand tailwind is present. |

**Where this differs from the score, and why:** the screen's `score` is a percentile rank built from revenue growth, earnings growth, and 6-month return — all metrics that mechanically reward companies coming off a smaller or depressed prior-year base. That is why **MU (score 93.9) ranks highest on the score but lowest on durability conviction here**, and why **TER (score 78.8)** also ranks near the bottom of the durability list. Conversely, **MSFT and AAPL (score 30.3, the lowest in the cohort)** rank near the top of the durability list, because their modest growth rates come from large, diversified, structurally entrenched businesses rather than a cyclical rebound. The score is a valid ordering of *this week's cohort by recent growth-and-return magnitude*; it is not a measure of how repeatable that magnitude is going forward, and the two orderings should be read as complementary, not interchangeable.

criteria.screen: Growth and momentum. No valuation, profitability or leverage filter.
criteria.free_cash_flow: Positive trailing free cash flow. The only quality guardrail in the screen — it separates growth that generates cash from growth that burns it.
criteria.trend: Price above the 50-day moving average, and the 50-day above the 200-day. The second is the underlying trend; the first alone can be a two-week bounce.
criteria.return_6m: Positive 6-month total return, on split- and dividend-adjusted prices.
criteria.excluded_on_purpose: There is no P/E, ROE or debt filter. In this index a P/E under 20 rejects almost the whole universe, and what it lets through is the least representative of what the index is. A low multiple here does not signal quality; it signals that the market has stopped expecting growth.
criteria.score: Within-cohort percentile rank, averaged over revenue growth, earnings growth and 6-month return. 100 means best of the names that passed this week, not best company — a name's score moves when the rest of the cohort moves. Ranks rather than raw values, so that one company emerging from a cyclical trough with triple-digit earnings growth cannot dominate the average.

valuation_method.model: Two-stage DCF on levered free cash flow (FCF discounted at cost of equity, compared with market cap — no net-debt bridge)
valuation_method.discount_rate: CAPM: currency-matched risk-free rate + beta x 5% ERP, beta clamped to [0.3, 2.5], rate clamped to [5%, 18%]. Only USD has a live quote (^TNX); other currencies use a documented static rate, flagged per company in risk_free_source.
valuation_method.implied_growth: Reverse DCF — the FCF growth rate that sets the model's equity value equal to today's market cap. What the price assumes, not a forecast. Available for every company, since it needs no history.
valuation_method.trend_test: A projection is only made when a least-squares line through log FCF reaches R2 >= 0.5. Below that the series is a path rather than a direction, dcf_value_per_share is null and dcf_skipped_reason says so.
valuation_method.probability: P(growth >= implied growth) under a Student-t fitted to the company's own year-on-year FCF growth in log space. Withheld entirely above a log stdev of 1.0, where it would be indistinguishable from a coin flip.
known_limits: History depth is uneven. SEC filings give US companies 14-17 years (16 growth observations for Adobe), but that source only covers SEC filers, so the IBEX screener and any company whose filing history has gaps falls back to yfinance's 4 years — 3 observations. Each company's fcf_source and probability.observations say which it got, and every probability is published as a range rather than a point.

A short FCF window can catch a trough, a spike or both and mistake it for a trend, and a long one can fit an earlier version of the company beautifully. The R2 test guards the first, and projecting the lower of the long-run and recent trends guards the second. Neither is a cure.
Terminal growth is a single 2.5% applied to every business regardless of its long-run ceiling; dcf_terminal_value_share_pct shows how much of each valuation rests on it.

The model sees free cash flow only — no revenue detail, margins, guidance or segments. A one-off legal settlement, licensing payment or deferred capex is indistinguishable from a genuine trend change, which is why revenue growth is carried alongside as a corroboration check.
Levered FCF is compared directly against market cap with no net-debt bridge — a deliberate simplification for data robustness across 500 tickers.

valuations.dcf_skipped_reason: free cash flow does not follow a trend (R2 0.32 < 0.5); projecting it would describe the path of the series, not the business

valuation_report:
# What the Market Is Paying For — A Reverse-DCF Read Across the Nasdaq-100 Quality Screen

The only number every one of these nine companies has in common is `implied_growth_pct` — the FCF growth rate that, run through a decade of explicit cash flows plus a 2.5% terminal value, reconciles today's market cap exactly. Everything else — historical CAGR, trend fit, revenue corroboration, probability — exists to answer one question: does this company's own cash-flow history make that assumption plausible, implausible, or simply unjudgeable?

---

## 1. Company by company: what's priced in, and whether it can be checked

**Teradyne (TER)** — Price implies **43.1%** annual FCF growth. The cash-flow series (16 years) has an R² of just **0.32** against a log-linear trend: this is a path, not a direction, and the 10-K history shows an endpoint CAGR of **-0.6%** and a recent trajectory of **-13.0%**. No gap can honestly be computed here — there is no trend to measure the 43.1% against. The DCF itself was withheld for the same reason.

**AMD** — The implied growth figure is **null**, flagged `above_model_range`: the price requires growth so far beyond what the reverse-DCF search space covers that the model cannot even name a number for it. That is itself the finding — an assumption too extreme to quantify, not a modest premium. Separately, a forward DCF was still run using the much more moderate *recent* trend growth (8.5%, against a longer-run trend of 41.5%, which itself is decelerating — `trend_broken` is true). On that basis alone, fair value comes to $18.16 against a $516.13 price, a **-96.5%** gap — but this is not a read on what the market is actually pricing in, since that figure is unknown.

**MRVL** — Price implies **51.9%** growth. The trend is real (R²=0.81) but points to **19.5%**, matched closely by the endpoint CAGR (21.1%). The gap is **+32.4 points** — the price is pricing in growth more than two-and-a-half times what the company's own five-year cash-flow trend supports. DCF value is $31.36 against $236.10 (**-86.7%** upside), with over 45% of that DCF resting on the terminal value.

**NVIDIA (NVDA)** — Price implies **40.8%** growth. The trend fit is very strong (R²=0.90), but it points to **186.2%** — a rate the model itself will not project (its band is capped at [-15%, 25%]), so the DCF was declined outright. The gap here (**-145.4 points**) cuts the opposite way from every other name in this set: the market is pricing in a sharp *deceleration* from the recent run rate, not an acceleration. The trend, however, rests on only four fiscal years, and FCF growth (100%+ implied by the base) diverges from revenue growth by **86 points** — a divergence too large to explain from cash-flow data alone.

**Palantir (PLTR)** — Price implies **54.8%** growth. Trend fit is solid (R²=0.82) at **74.8%**, so the gap is **-19.9 points**: the market is again pricing in deceleration relative to the recent trend, not confirmation of it. The trend itself spans six years, one of them cash-flow negative, and FCF growth diverges from revenue growth by **41.8 points**. The DCF was declined because trend growth (74.8%) sits outside the projectable band.

**Amazon (AMZN)** — Price implies **37.1%** growth. R² is **0.579** — just above the threshold used here, but `trend_recent_pct` is **-51.1%** against a longer trend of 23.4%, and `trend_broken` is flagged true. This is a trend that is nominally "real" by the R² cutoff but visibly breaking down in its most recent behaviour; a **+13.7 point** gap computed against the 23.4% figure should be read with that instability in mind rather than as a clean signal. The DCF was withheld because the recent growth used for projection falls outside the modelled band.

**Analog Devices (ADI)** — Price implies **22.5%** growth against a well-supported trend of **14.7%** (R²=0.89, endpoint CAGR a corroborating 16.4%) — a **+7.8 point** gap, the smallest positive gap in the set. Revenue growth is actually **negative** (-2.8%) while FCF trend growth is positive, a **17.5-point** divergence that the cash-flow data cannot explain (it could be margin, mix, or something non-recurring — no claim is made either way). DCF value is $157.25 against $378.78 (**-58.5%**), over half of it from the terminal value.

**Apple (AAPL)** — Price implies **20.4%** growth against a trend of **12.4%** (R²=0.77) — a **+8.0 point** gap. The most recent year's growth has flattened to **0.98%** (`trend_broken` true), and revenue growth of 1.8% lags the FCF trend by 10.5 points. DCF value is $81.68 against $332.27 (**-75.4%**).

**Microsoft (MSFT)** — Price implies **21.9%** growth against a trend of **8.7%** (R²=0.89) — the largest gap among the fully-computed names at **+13.2 points**. Revenue growth (16.1%) actually *exceeds* the FCF trend, a rare negative divergence (-7.5pp) worth flagging. DCF value is $121.59 against $495.63 (**-75.5%**), with 47% of that value sitting in the terminal term.

---

## 2. Which cash flows support a projection — and which don't

**Trend-like enough to compare against (R² ≥ 0.5):** AMD, MRVL, NVDA, PLTR, AMZN, ADI, AAPL, MSFT. For all eight, the gap between implied and trend growth is at least arithmetically meaningful — though for NVDA, PLTR and AMZN, the model still declined to publish a DCF value because the trend growth itself sits outside the [-15%, 25%] band it is willing to extrapolate. That refusal is a finding: it says the trend, however statistically clean, describes a growth rate the model considers unprojectable over a ten-year horizon, not that the company lacks a trend.

**Not trend-like (R² < 0.5):** Teradyne alone. Its 16-year FCF series has an R² of 0.32 — below the level at which a line through the data means anything. The 43.1% implied growth figure stands on its own, uncorroborated by any usable historical direction, and no gap, no DCF, and no ranking against the other eight names is offered for it.

---

## 3. Reading the probabilities as ranges, not points

Every probability here is a Student-t estimate on a small sample (`observations` ranging from 3 to 16), and per the methodology it should be quoted as the `probability_range_pct` band, not the point estimate:

- **TER**: 18.2%–26.6% (15 obs) — historically, growth this fast or faster was uncommon.
- **AMD**: no usable estimate — implied growth itself is unresolved, so there is nothing to compare a historical distribution against.
- **MRVL**: 12.0%–29.1% (only 4 obs) — a wide band on a thin sample.
- **NVDA**: 70.3%–90.0% (3 obs) — high, because NVDA's own trailing growth has repeatedly exceeded 40%, but three data points cannot support precision.
- **PLTR**: 51.1%–52.6% (4 obs) — an unusually narrow band for so few observations; still built on four data points.
- **AMZN**: 37.0%–41.5% (12 obs) — a reasonably sized sample given the volatility already flagged in its trend.
- **ADI**: 43.1%–45.2% (16 obs) — the most observations in the set, so the most trustworthy band here.
- **AAPL**: 43.4%–45.4% (16 obs) — likewise well-sampled.
- **MSFT**: 13.0%–21.6% (16 obs) — well-sampled, and the lowest band of the group with a comparably sized sample, meaning MSFT's own FCF history has rarely grown at the rate its price now implies.

A high band (NVDA, PLTR) says that company's own past cleared that growth bar often — it says nothing about whether it will again. A low band (MSFT, TER) says the opposite: history rarely got there. Neither is a forecast.

---

## 4. Where this model is most likely to be wrong

- **Sample size.** Most probability estimates rest on 3–6 year-on-year growth observations (MRVL: 4, NVDA: 3, PLTR: 4, AMD: 6). A Student-t fit on that few points produces wide, unstable bands almost by construction — the ranges quoted above should be treated as rough brackets, not precision estimates, even where the arithmetic looks tidy.

- **Short windows on cyclical or newly-scaled businesses.** NVDA's trend is built on four fiscal years that happen to coincide with an unprecedented demand cycle; a fifth year of moderation or contraction would move `trend_r2` and the implied comparison substantially. The same applies to MRVL (5 years) and PLTR (6 years). A model that only sees four to six data points cannot distinguish a structural re-rating from the up-leg of a cycle.

- **One terminal growth rate for every business.** The 2.5% perpetuity assumption is applied identically to a semiconductor equipment maker (TER), a chipmaker at the center of an AI buildout (NVDA), a software-defined data-and-analytics firm (PLTR), and a mature consumer-hardware franchise (AAPL). Where `dcf_terminal_value_share_pct` is high — 54% for ADI, 47% for MSFT and AAPL, 46% for MRVL — roughly half or more of the entire valuation rests on that single, business-agnostic number, not on anything specific to the company.

- **Cash flow without context.** The model reads FCF and nothing else. It cannot tell a legal settlement from a licensing payment, a deferred capex cycle from a genuine margin structural shift, or a one-off working-capital swing from a repeatable pattern. Several of the corroboration checks above flag exactly this kind of ambiguity — ADI's negative revenue growth against positive FCF growth, MSFT's FCF trend lagging its revenue growth, NVDA's and PLTR's FCF growth running far ahead of revenue — without the data to say which explanation applies. Divergence is reported here as a flag, not a diagnosis.

This is a description of what today's prices assume and how that assumption compares with each company's own cash-flow history — not a judgment on whether any of these businesses are good investments, and not a recommendation to buy, sell, or hold any of them.
